solution.concept_anchor: Article 123 subject-matter jurisdiction
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because students conflate the President's general executive authority over all three lists with the specific legislative substitute power under Article 123, which is limited to Union and Concurrent Lists only.
elimination_logic: Eliminate any option that includes the State List — Article 123 ordinance power is restricted to Union and Concurrent List subjects, not State List subjects.
Eliminate any option claiming all three lists are covered — this is the classic scope-extension trap; the President has no ordinance power over State List.
Confirm that Union List and Concurrent List alone define the subject-matter jurisdiction of Article 123 — select option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who know the President is the supreme executive authority sometimes assume that his ordinance power mirrors his executive power and extends to all legislative matters including the State List. The trap is a scope-extension error: Article 123 grants a legislative substitute power, not an executive power, and it is confined to subjects on which Parliament itself can legislate — the Union List and the Concurrent List. The State List belongs exclusively to State Legislatures, so neither Parliament nor the President's ordinance can reach it.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 123 empowers the President to promulgate ordinances during the recess of Parliament, but only on subjects over which Parliament itself has legislative competence. Parliament's competence is defined by the Seventh Schedule, covering the Union List (List I) and the Concurrent List (List III). The State List (List II) is reserved for State Legislatures, and neither Parliament by statute nor the President by ordinance can legislate on those subjects in normal circumstances.

• Option (a) — Union List only: Too narrow; the Concurrent List is equally within Parliament's reach, so ordinances can cover it too.
• Option (b) — Union List and Concurrent List only: Correct. This precisely maps ordinance power to Parliament's competence.
• Option (c) — All three Lists: Incorrect. The State List is outside Parliament's and therefore the President's ordinance jurisdiction.
• Option (d) — Concurrent List only: Too narrow; excludes the Union List, which is Parliament's primary domain.

Value Addition:
• On Concurrent List subjects, a Presidential ordinance prevails over inconsistent State law — the same supremacy rule as Article 254 for Acts.
• During a National Emergency (Article 352), Parliament's power expands to the State List, correspondingly expanding the ordinance power.
• Governor's ordinance under Article 213 is similarly confined to subjects within State Legislature's competence.

concepts_used: Preconditions for Promulgation: 'Satisfaction' of the President
Re-promulgation of Ordinances: The DC Wadhwa Doctrine

solution.concept_anchor: DC Wadhwa doctrine and presidential satisfaction

statement_analysis.statement: In DC Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987), the Supreme Court held that the repeated re-promulgation of ordinances without placing them before the legislature amounts to a fraud on the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court in DC Wadhwa (1987) explicitly ruled that re-promulgating ordinances to avoid legislative scrutiny subverts parliamentary democracy and constitutes a fraud on the Constitution.

statement_analysis.statement: The 'satisfaction' required of the President under Article 123 is purely subjective and wholly immune from any form of judicial review.
statement_analysis.reason: In AK Roy v. Union of India (1982) and later confirmed in Krishna Kumar Singh (2017), the Supreme Court held that presidential satisfaction is not immune from judicial review — courts can examine whether it was bona fide, though they are reluctant to interfere in genuine urgency cases.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 74, the Council of Ministers' advice binds the President in the exercise of his ordinance-making power, especially after the 44th Constitutional Amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: The 44th Amendment (1978) made Cabinet advice binding on the President without any discretionary exception, including for ordinances — the ordinance is effectively a Cabinet decision expressed through the President.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (1 and 3 only) is deceptive because statement 2 sounds authoritative; students who partially know that presidential satisfaction has some subjective element may accept it as wholly immune, overlooking the judicial review dimension established in AK Roy.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 2: 'wholly immune from judicial review' — AK Roy (1982) and Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) both held that presidential satisfaction IS reviewable; eliminate options that include Statement 2 as correct.
Confirm Statement 1: DC Wadhwa (1987) explicitly called repeated re-promulgation a 'fraud on the Constitution' — this is a well-established ruling; Statement 1 is correct.
Confirm Statement 3: The 44th Amendment made Cabinet advice binding on the President for all executive actions including ordinances — Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The phrase 'purely subjective and wholly immune' in Statement 2 is a scope-extension trap. Students who know that presidential satisfaction has a subjective dimension (courts do not second-guess genuine executive judgment) incorrectly extend this to mean total immunity from judicial review. The actual position — established by AK Roy (1982) — is that courts can review whether the satisfaction was bona fide, even if they rarely intervene. A student who recalls only the 'satisfaction = subjective' half will accept Statement 2 as correct and choose option c instead of the correct option b.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 123 conditions the ordinance on the President being 'satisfied' that circumstances exist requiring immediate action. Three related dimensions are tested here.

• Statement 1 — Correct: In DC Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987), Bihar had re-promulgated numerous ordinances session after session without placing them before the legislature. The Supreme Court termed this a 'parallel legislature' and a fraud on the Constitution, since ordinances are meant to be a temporary measure, not a permanent substitute for legislation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Presidential satisfaction is not wholly immune from judicial review. In AK Roy v. Union of India (1982), the Supreme Court held that while courts are reluctant to interfere with genuine executive urgency, the satisfaction must be bona fide. Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) reinforced this, allowing courts to examine whether circumstances genuinely warranted an ordinance.
• Statement 3 — Correct: After the 44th Amendment (1978), the President is constitutionally bound by the Council of Ministers' advice under Article 74 in all matters, including ordinance promulgation. The political accountability for an ordinance thus rests with the Cabinet.

Value Addition:
• Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) is a seven-judge bench decision — the highest judicial pronouncement on ordinance power to date.
• Re-promulgation without legislative scrutiny violates the separation of powers and parliamentary accountability norms.
• The 44th Amendment removed the President's discretion to return Cabinet advice even once before promulgating an ordinance.

concepts_used: Condition of Parliamentary Recess

solution.concept_anchor: Recess condition — both Houses vs. at least one House

statement_analysis.statement: An ordinance under Article 123 can be promulgated only when both Houses of Parliament are in recess simultaneously.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 123 requires that Parliament (Houses) is not in session — this means at least one House is not in session; both Houses need not be in recess simultaneously as a strict conjunctive requirement, though in practice both Houses are usually in recess when ordinances are issued.

statement_analysis.statement: Prorogation, adjournment, and dissolution are legally equivalent triggers for the ordinance-making power under Article 123.
statement_analysis.reason: Prorogation ends a session and is the most common trigger; adjournment only suspends a sitting within a session and does not give rise to ordinance power; dissolution ends the life of the Lok Sabha and is a distinct situation — the three are not legally equivalent triggers.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because Statement 1 sounds like a reasonable reading of the constitutional text ('Houses are not in session'), and many students assume both Houses must simultaneously be in recess, which is the most common real-world scenario even if not the precise legal requirement.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The precise condition is that the Houses 'are not in session' — this does not require a strict simultaneous recess of BOTH Houses; Statement 1 over-states the requirement and is NOT correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Adjournment merely suspends a sitting within a session — it does not create the 'not in session' condition for ordinance power; the three terms are not legally equivalent triggers; Statement 2 is also NOT correct.
Both statements are incorrect — the question asks which are NOT correct — select option c (Both 1 and 2).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 1 exploits the common-sense assumption that 'not in session' necessarily means 'both Houses simultaneously in recess.' In practice, ordinances are issued when both Houses are in recess, making this assumption feel correct. However, the constitutional text is worded around the Houses not being in session, not around a strict simultaneous recess of both Houses. Statement 2 traps students who memorise 'prorogation, adjournment, dissolution' as a trio without distinguishing their legal effects — adjournment does not create the legislative vacuum that justifies executive ordinance-making.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 123 conditions ordinance power on Parliament not being in session — a deceptively simple phrase that conceals important nuances tested in this question.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: While it is true that ordinances are typically issued when both Houses are in recess, the constitutional condition is not a strict 'both Houses simultaneously in recess' requirement. The text says Houses 'are not in session.' The legally operative situation is that Parliament cannot be convened quickly to address the urgent matter.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The three terms — prorogation, adjournment, and dissolution — are legally distinct. Prorogation ends a session and is the normal trigger for ordinance power. Adjournment merely suspends a sitting within a continuing session and does NOT give rise to ordinance power; Parliament is still technically 'in session.' Dissolution ends Lok Sabha's life and creates a unique constitutional situation for ordinances.

Value Addition:
• During adjournment, Parliament is still 'in session' — no ordinance can be issued.
• After dissolution, an ordinance must be laid before the newly constituted Lok Sabha when it first meets.
• A Joint Sitting under Article 118 is a session of Parliament — ordinance power is not available during a Joint Sitting.

Ordinance and Constitutional Amendments: The Absolute Bar

solution.concept_anchor: Limits on ordinance legal force — constitutional amendment bar

statement_analysis.statement: A Presidential ordinance has the same legal force as an Act of Parliament during the period of its currency.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 123 explicitly states that an ordinance 'shall have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament' — it is not subordinate legislation.

statement_analysis.statement: A Presidential ordinance can be used to amend or repeal an existing Act of Parliament while it remains in operation.
statement_analysis.reason: Since an ordinance has the same force as a parliamentary Act, it can amend or repeal existing Acts during its currency — this is a direct consequence of its equal legal standing.

statement_analysis.statement: A Presidential ordinance can amend the Constitution if the amendment does not require ratification by State Legislatures.
statement_analysis.reason: An ordinance cannot amend the Constitution under any circumstances — Article 368 requires a special majority through the legislative process, and ordinance power is a 'legislative substitute,' not 'constituent power.' The distinction drawn in the statement about ratification is irrelevant; the bar is absolute.

statement_analysis.statement: A Presidential ordinance is subject to the same fundamental rights limitations as an ordinary law and can be struck down under Article 13.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 13 defines 'law' to include ordinances; hence an ordinance that violates Part III rights is void to the extent of the inconsistency — it has no special immunity from fundamental rights review.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Only three) is a strong distractor because Statement 3 contains a seemingly reasonable qualifier ('if ratification is not required'), and students who partially know the constitutional amendment bar may believe partial amendments without state ratification could be done by ordinance.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 123 explicitly gives ordinances 'the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament' — Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Equal legal force means an ordinance can amend or repeal Acts during its currency — Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: The bar on using ordinances to amend the Constitution is absolute — it applies regardless of whether state ratification is required; Statement 3 is incorrect.

Evaluate Statement 4: Article 13's definition of 'law' includes ordinances — they are subject to Part III scrutiny; Statement 4 is correct. Three statements are correct — select option c (Only three).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the precision trap. Students who know the constitutional amendment bar may recall that it exists 'because state ratification is required' for certain amendments, and then reason that amendments not requiring ratification might be achievable by ordinance. This reasoning is flawed: the bar is not derived from the ratification requirement but from the fundamental distinction between constituent power (Article 368) and legislative power (Article 123). No ordinance can exercise constituent power under any circumstances.
solution.final_explanation:
The legal status of a Presidential ordinance — what it can and cannot do — is a high-frequency UPSC testing area.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 123 explicitly equates the ordinance's force with that of a parliamentary Act during its operation. It is not subordinate legislation like a rule or notification.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Since an ordinance equals an Act in force, it can amend or repeal existing parliamentary Acts while it is in operation — a power that distinguishes it from mere executive orders.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The ordinance-to-constitutional amendment bar is absolute. Article 368 requires special legislative procedure (special majority, and sometimes state ratification) to exercise constituent power. An ordinance exercises legislative power — it cannot cross into constituent territory regardless of whether the specific amendment requires state ratification.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Article 13(3)(a) defines 'law' broadly to include any ordinance. An ordinance violating fundamental rights is void to the extent of the violation — it enjoys no special immunity.

Value Addition:
• The same Article 13 logic means ordinances are also subject to review under Articles 14, 19, and 21.
• An ordinance can be converted into a permanent Act if Parliament passes it before expiry.
• 'Legislative substitute' vs. 'constituent power' is the key conceptual divide explaining why ordinances cannot amend the Constitution.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 123 vs. Article 213 — comparative features
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because it correctly pairs A and B but swaps the entries for C and D, exploiting student confusion about which authority (President vs. Governor) has oversight over the other's ordinances.
elimination_logic: Match A (Article 123) with its correct feature: Article 123 governs Presidential ordinances — paired with '2' (ordinance on Union and Concurrent List subjects during Parliament's recess).

Match B (Article 213) with its correct feature: Article 213 governs Governor's ordinances — the Governor CANNOT issue an ordinance on certain subjects without Presidential instructions; paired with '4' (requires Presidential instructions for specified subjects).
Match C: Presidential direction to withdraw — the President can direct the Governor to withdraw a state ordinance; paired with '1'.
Match D: Same 6-week validity after reassembly applies to both Article 123 and Article 213 — paired with '3'. Correct combination is A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 — select option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap targets students who mix up which authority has oversight over which ordinance. Many students know the President can direct the Governor to withdraw an ordinance but incorrectly attribute this power to the Governor over Presidential ordinances. Similarly, the 6-week validity period is identical for both Article 123 and Article 213, which is a deliberate same-period trap — students who think the periods differ will mis-match entry D.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 123 and 213 govern Presidential and Governor's ordinance powers respectively. Comparing them is a standard UPSC technique.

Correct matches: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3.

• A (Article 123) — 2: The President's ordinance power covers Union and Concurrent List subjects during Parliament's recess — the foundational scope provision.
• B (Article 213) — 4: The Governor cannot issue an ordinance on subjects such as compulsory acquisition of property or matters affecting the High Court without Presidential instructions — a critical limitation that has no parallel in Article 123.
• C (Presidential direction to withdraw state ordinance) — 1: The President can direct a Governor to withdraw a state ordinance. No reverse relationship exists — a Governor cannot direct withdrawal of a Presidential ordinance.
• D (6-week validity after reassembly) — 3: Both Article 123 and Article 213 ordinances cease to operate 6 weeks after the respective legislature reassembles — the identical period is a common MCQ trap designed to make students think they differ.

Value Addition:
• Governor's ordinances on certain subjects must be reserved for Presidential consideration — analogous to Bills under Article 200.
• The President has no obligation to reserve his own ordinances for any authority's consideration.
• If both Houses of Parliament reassemble on different dates, the 6-week period starts from the LATER date.

Expiry and Validity Period of an Ordinance

solution.concept_anchor: 6-week validity — later date rule for different reassembly dates
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually correct, and students who know both facts may still assume the causal link is merely incidental rather than recognising that the 'later date' rule directly operationalises the mandatory laying requirement for both Houses.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Article 123(2) mandates that when both Houses reassemble on different dates, the 6-week period is counted from the later date, ensuring both Houses have an opportunity to act on the ordinance.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Article 123(2) explicitly requires the ordinance to be laid before both Houses of Parliament, not just one.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The 'later date' rule exists precisely because laying is mandatory before BOTH Houses; if the period started from the earlier date, the House that reassembles later might have no meaningful opportunity to disapprove the ordinance. R is the direct constitutional rationale for the rule stated in A.
Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A — select option a.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 123(2) contains two interlocking rules: the mandatory laying requirement before both Houses, and the 6-week validity period measured from the later reassembly date when Houses reassemble on different days.

• Assertion (A) is correct: When both Houses reassemble on different dates, the 6-week countdown for the ordinance's validity begins from the date the second House reassembles — the later date. This is the unambiguous constitutional text.
• Reason (R) is correct: Article 123(2) mandates laying the ordinance before both Houses of Parliament — not just one. This is a mandatory procedural requirement, not discretionary.
• Causal link: R explains A directly. The 'later date' rule exists to protect the constitutional right of both Houses to consider the ordinance. If the clock started from the earlier reassembly date, the House reconvening later might have fewer than 6 weeks — or no time at all — to pass a resolution of disapproval. The mandatory laying before both Houses thus necessitates the later-date measurement rule.

Value Addition:
• An ordinance can also cease before 6 weeks if both Houses pass resolutions of disapproval.
• Laying is mandatory, but parliamentary approval is not automatic — Parliament may let the ordinance lapse or actively disapprove it.
• The President can also withdraw the ordinance before the 6-week period ends — a separate mode of cessation.

solution.concept_anchor: Sequence of events in ordinance lifecycle
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is a strong distractor because it correctly places promulgation before Parliament reassembling but reverses the withdrawal and disapproval sequence, exploiting confusion about whether executive withdrawal or legislative disapproval is the primary cessation mechanism.
elimination_logic: Promulgation is the starting point — it must come first chronologically; eliminate any sequence that does not begin with promulgation.
Parliament reassembling follows promulgation — the ordinance is then laid before both Houses; this is the next step.
Parliamentary disapproval (resolution by both Houses) is a possible cessation event that occurs after reassembly during the 6-week window.

Presidential withdrawal can happen at any time, including before Parliament reassembles — it is not necessarily the last event; the correct sequence is: Promulgation → Parliament reassembles → Laying before both Houses → Disapproval resolution / 6-week expiry. Among the given options, option b correctly sequences: Promulgation → Reassembly → Laying → 6-week expiry as the standard lifecycle without disapproval — select option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap targets students who know the events of the ordinance lifecycle but confuse their sequence. Presidential withdrawal can occur at any time — even before Parliament reassembles — while disapproval can only occur after Parliament reassembles. Students often place withdrawal after disapproval, treating them as sequential alternatives rather than independent cessation mechanisms available at different stages.
solution.final_explanation:
The lifecycle of a Presidential ordinance follows a constitutionally mandated sequence under Article 123.

Correct sequence: Promulgation of ordinance → Parliament reassembles → Ordinance laid before both Houses → Either (i) both Houses pass disapproval resolutions (ceases immediately), (ii) 6-week period elapses without approval (ceases automatically), or (iii) President withdraws (ceases immediately).

• Option (a): Places disapproval before laying — incorrect; disapproval can only occur after laying, which happens after reassembly.
• Option (b): Correct. Promulgation precedes reassembly; laying is the first post-reassembly step; 6-week expiry is the default cessation mechanism if Parliament takes no action.
• Option (c): Reverses disapproval and 6-week expiry — incorrect; disapproval occurs within the 6-week window, not after it.
• Option (d): Places withdrawal after 6-week expiry — incorrect; withdrawal can occur at any time, including before Parliament reassembles.

Value Addition:
• Presidential withdrawal under Article 123(2)(b) is prospective — it does not revive laws repealed by the ordinance during its currency.
• Acts done during the ordinance's operation remain valid even after the ordinance ceases, unless a court strikes them down.
• Governor's ordinance under Article 213 follows the same lifecycle sequence with respect to the State Legislature.

Ordinance vs. Act of Parliament: Key Distinctions

solution.concept_anchor: Ordinance disapproval — prospective effect and no Presidential assent
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students familiar with the Presidential assent requirement for Bills automatically transpose it to the ordinance disapproval context, not realising that disapproval is a legislative act of rejection that does not go back to the President.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: Ordinance disapproval does NOT require Presidential assent — it is a legislative rejection, unlike a Bill which requires presidential assent to become law.
Eliminate option b: The Rajya Sabha has equal power to disapprove — no special privilege is granted to the Lok Sabha in ordinance disapproval proceedings.
Eliminate option d: Both Houses must pass resolutions of disapproval — one House alone cannot terminate the ordinance; a resolution by Rajya Sabha alone is insufficient.

Confirm option c: The disapproval is prospective — licenses already granted under the ordinance remain valid; the ordinance ceases going forward but past actions under it are not automatically invalidated. Select option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap exploits the instinctive association between 'legislation' and 'Presidential assent.' Students who know that Bills require Presidential assent to become Acts incorrectly apply this logic to ordinance disapproval, reasoning that the President must somehow consent to his own ordinance being rejected. In reality, disapproval is a constitutional power of Parliament to reject executive legislation — it operates without any executive co-signature, unlike the ordinary legislative process.
solution.final_explanation:
An ordinance promulgating a licensing scheme is in force. Both Houses pass resolutions disapproving it within the 6-week window. The question is: what is the correct constitutional position regarding licences already issued under that ordinance?

The applicable principle is the prospective effect of ordinance disapproval under Article 123(2). When Parliament passes resolutions of disapproval, the ordinance ceases to operate from the date of disapproval — not retrospectively. Acts already done, rights already accrued, and licences already granted under the ordinance remain legally valid unless a court separately strikes them down.

• Option (a): Disapproval does NOT require Presidential assent — incorrect; it is a direct legislative act, not a Bill requiring assent.
• Option (b): Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha have equal power in ordinance disapproval — no special Lok Sabha privilege exists here.
• Option (c): Correct. Disapproval is prospective; licences already issued under the ordinance remain valid. The ordinance ceases operating going forward.
• Option (d): Both Houses must pass disapproval resolutions — a single House cannot terminate an ordinance unilaterally.

Value Addition:
• The prospective effect rule protects third-party rights created under the ordinance before its disapproval.
• An ordinance can also be converted into an Act before disapproval if Parliament passes it.
• The 44th Amendment's binding Cabinet advice rule means the Cabinet, not the President, bears political accountability for the ordinance.

solution.concept_anchor: Absolute bars on Presidential ordinance power
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because students who know that ordinances cannot override fundamental rights think 'reasonable restriction under Article 19(2)' is an absolute bar, not realising that an ordinance imposing reasonable restrictions is constitutionally valid — it is the violation of fundamental rights that is barred, not all engagement with Part III.
elimination_logic: Check option a: Constitutional amendment under Article 368 — requires Special Majority through legislative process; ordinance cannot do this; a genuine bar.

Check option b: Imposing reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) — ordinances imposing reasonable restrictions on freedom of speech are valid law; this is NOT an absolute bar; it is a permissible ordinance action.
Check option c: Ratification by State Legislatures — ordinance cannot bypass provisions requiring state ratification; a genuine bar.
Check option d: Matters exclusively in the State List — ordinance cannot be issued on State List subjects in normal circumstances; a genuine bar.

Option b is the odd one out — it is not a bar on ordinance-making power but rather a permissible subject. However, re-reading the question: which does NOT belong to the category of matters on which an ordinance CANNOT be issued — option b (reasonable restrictions) is the one that CAN be done by ordinance. But options a, c, d are all genuine bars. The odd one out among the 'cannot be issued' group is b — select option b... Re-check: Question asks which does NOT belong to the list of things an ordinance CANNOT do — meaning which CAN be done. Option b (reasonable restrictions) CAN be done by ordinance. Correct answer is b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges two related but distinct concepts: (1) ordinances that violate fundamental rights are void, and (2) ordinances that deal with subject-matter touching fundamental rights are void. The first proposition is correct; the second is not. An ordinance that imposes a reasonable restriction on free speech under Article 19(2) is constitutionally valid — the reasonable restriction doctrine applies equally to ordinances as to Acts. Students who conflate 'touching fundamental rights' with 'violating fundamental rights' will incorrectly identify option b as a bar.
solution.final_explanation:
Three of the four options identify genuine constitutional bars on Presidential ordinance power; one identifies something an ordinance CAN lawfully do.

• Option (a) — Genuine bar: Constitutional amendment under Article 368 requires a special legislative procedure — special majority, and sometimes state ratification. Ordinance power is legislative substitute power, not constituent power; this bar is absolute.
• Option (b) — NOT a bar (odd one out): An ordinance imposing reasonable restrictions on fundamental rights (e.g., restrictions on free speech under Article 19(2) in the interest of public order) is constitutionally valid. What is barred is an ordinance that violates fundamental rights — not one that lawfully engages with them.
• Option (c) — Genuine bar: Provisions requiring ratification by not less than half of State Legislatures (certain constitutional amendments) cannot be bypassed by an ordinance.
• Option (d) — Genuine bar: State List subjects fall outside Parliament's legislative competence in normal circumstances; ordinances similarly cannot reach them.

Value Addition:
• Article 13(3) includes ordinances within the definition of 'law,' making Part III fully applicable.
• During National Emergency, the State List becomes accessible to Parliament — and correspondingly to Presidential ordinance power.
• The reasonable restriction jurisprudence under Articles 19(2)–19(6) applies identically to ordinances and Acts.

solution.concept_anchor: Withdrawal vs. disapproval — effects on prior acts

statement_analysis.statement: When the President withdraws an ordinance under Article 123(2)(b), any law that was repealed by that ordinance during its currency is automatically revived upon withdrawal.
statement_analysis.reason: Presidential withdrawal of an ordinance has prospective effect only — it does not revive laws repealed or amended during the ordinance's currency; those repeals remain in effect unless separately re-enacted.

statement_analysis.statement: For an ordinance to cease due to parliamentary disapproval, resolutions to that effect must be passed by both Houses of Parliament, and such disapproval does not require Presidential assent.
statement_analysis.reason: Both Houses must pass disapproval resolutions; a single House cannot kill an ordinance. Crucially, unlike a Bill, ordinance disapproval does not require Presidential assent — it is a direct legislative act of rejection.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students who know Statement 2 is correct may assume Statement 1 is also correct by analogising withdrawal to 'undoing' the ordinance in its entirety, not realising that withdrawal has prospective-only effect.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Withdrawal of an ordinance does NOT revive previously repealed laws — withdrawal operates prospectively only; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Both Houses must pass disapproval resolutions, and Presidential assent is NOT required — this is the correct position; Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct — select option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits a partial-truth trap: students know withdrawal 'undoes' the ordinance going forward but incorrectly extend this to mean it 'undoes' the ordinance's past effects, including laws it repealed. The correct rule — that withdrawal is prospective only — means the legal landscape changed by the ordinance stays changed even after withdrawal. Students who think of withdrawal as a 'reset button' will wrongly accept Statement 1.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests two distinct cessation mechanisms for Presidential ordinances and their legal effects.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Presidential withdrawal under Article 123(2)(b) has prospective effect. If an ordinance repealed an earlier Act during its currency, that repeal is not undone by withdrawal. The earlier Act does not revive automatically — separate legislative action would be needed to restore it. Treating withdrawal as a retrospective undoing is the classic error here.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Parliamentary disapproval requires resolutions from both Houses — neither House alone can terminate an ordinance. More importantly, this disapproval does not require Presidential assent. Unlike the normal legislative process where a Bill needs the President's signature to become law, ordinance disapproval is a direct constitutional power of Parliament exercised without executive co-participation.

Value Addition:
• Withdrawal is an executive act; disapproval is a legislative act — the two are conceptually and procedurally distinct.
• After disapproval, acts already done under the ordinance remain valid unless a court separately strikes them down.
• The President cannot theoretically refuse to withdraw an ordinance if the Cabinet advises withdrawal, given Article 74.

solution.concept_anchor: Krishna Kumar Singh 2017 — seven-judge bench ruling
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because DC Wadhwa (1987) is the original and more famous ordinance re-promulgation case; students who remember that case as the definitive precedent on re-promulgation may not know that Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) is a higher-authority seven-judge bench ruling that consolidated and extended the doctrine.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a (DC Wadhwa, 1987): DC Wadhwa was a two/three-judge bench ruling — it was a significant precedent but not a seven-judge bench; the blank requires the seven-judge bench case.
Eliminate option c (AK Roy, 1982): AK Roy addressed presidential satisfaction and judicial review, not specifically re-promulgation by a seven-judge bench.
Eliminate option d (SR Bommai, 1994): SR Bommai is a nine-judge bench ruling on Article 356 / President's Rule, not on ordinance re-promulgation.
Confirm option b (Krishna Kumar Singh, 2017): This is the seven-judge Constitution Bench ruling that comprehensively held re-promulgation of ordinances to be unconstitutional — select option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap here substitutes Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) with DC Wadhwa (1987). Both cases deal with ordinance re-promulgation, and DC Wadhwa is the more widely recalled case. However, Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) is the seven-judge Constitution Bench decision — a higher-authority ruling that definitively settled the constitutional position on re-promulgation. Students who associate 'fraud on Constitution' exclusively with DC Wadhwa will choose option a without knowing that the seven-judge bench specification points to the 2017 case.
solution.final_explanation:
The Supreme Court has addressed ordinance re-promulgation in two landmark rulings.

• Option (a) — DC Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987): The original ruling calling repeated re-promulgation a 'fraud on the Constitution.' A significant precedent, but NOT a seven-judge Constitution Bench — it was decided by a smaller bench.
• Option (b) — Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017): Correct. A seven-judge Constitution Bench comprehensively addressed ordinance re-promulgation, holding it unconstitutional and reinforcing that the President and Governor cannot use repeated re-promulgation to bypass legislative scrutiny. It examined the bona fides of presidential satisfaction and the doctrine of constitutional morality in the context of executive ordinance power.
• Option (c) — AK Roy v. Union of India (1982): Addressed judicial review of presidential satisfaction under Article 123 — not a seven-judge bench ruling on re-promulgation.
• Option (d) — SR Bommai v. Union of India (1994): A nine-judge bench ruling on Article 356 and President's Rule — unrelated to ordinance re-promulgation.

Value Addition:
• Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) is currently the highest judicial pronouncement on ordinance power.
• The ruling distinguished between a single ordinance (constitutionally permissible) and serial re-promulgation (unconstitutional).
• Constitutional morality — not just legal validity — is a key analytical tool the Court applied in Krishna Kumar Singh.

solution.concept_anchor: Presidential ordinance power expansion under Article 356
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d is a strong distractor because students know that during National Emergency (Article 352), Parliament's power expands to include State List subjects; they may recall this fact but incorrectly think it means the ordinance power automatically expands without the Article 356 route being a separate valid mechanism.
elimination_logic: Evaluate option a: Under Article 356 (President's Rule), the President exercises the powers of the State Legislature — he can issue ordinances for the State as well; this is a correctly matched pair.

Evaluate option b: A Presidential ordinance on a Concurrent List subject does NOT require state government consent — the Union's legislative supremacy on Concurrent List applies equally to ordinances; this pair is incorrectly matched.

Evaluate option c: State cannot independently re-legislate on a Concurrent List subject if a Presidential ordinance already occupies the field — this is not a concurrent power; the pair is incorrectly matched.

Evaluate option d: Ordinance power expansion during National Emergency is through Parliament gaining State List competence — it does not suspend the preconditions of Article 123; this pair is incorrectly matched. Option a is the correctly matched pair — select option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges two distinct mechanisms of central legislative expansion — Article 352 (National Emergency) and Article 356 (President's Rule). Students who know one often confuse the route by which central ordinance power expands. Under Article 356, the President directly assumes the State Legislature's functions and can issue ordinances for the State. Under Article 352, Parliament's competence expands to the State List, but this is different from exercising State Legislature powers. Students who conflate these two routes will evaluate option a incorrectly.
solution.final_explanation:
Presidential ordinance power intersects with federal architecture in important ways.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: Under Article 356 (President's Rule), the President assumes the functions of the State Legislature. This means the President can issue ordinances for that State — extending beyond the normal Union/Concurrent List jurisdiction to cover State matters. This is a well-established constitutional position.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: A Presidential ordinance on a Concurrent List subject does not require state government consent. The same supremacy rule that applies to central Acts under Article 254 applies to Presidential ordinances — state consent is not a precondition.
• Option (c) — Incorrectly matched: A State cannot independently legislate on a Concurrent List subject where a Presidential ordinance already occupies the field — the field occupation doctrine applies to ordinances just as to Acts.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: During National Emergency, Parliament gains State List competence — but the Article 123 preconditions (Parliament not in session, etc.) still apply; the Emergency does not suspend the ordinance procedure.

Value Addition:
• Under Article 356, the President legislates for a State through Parliament making laws or by Presidential ordinance — both routes are available.
• 'Field occupation' by a Presidential ordinance on Concurrent List subjects blocks contradictory state ordinances too.
• Article 357 regulates Parliament's exercise of State List powers during President's Rule.

Constitutional Basis and Scope of Article 123

solution.concept_anchor: 44th Amendment — Cabinet binding; ordinance as Cabinet decision

statement_analysis.statement: Prior to the 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978), the President had a degree of personal discretion in deciding whether to promulgate an ordinance even when the Cabinet recommended it.
statement_analysis.reason: Before the 44th Amendment, Article 74 allowed the President to seek reconsideration of Cabinet advice once — this element of discretion, while limited, existed in the original framework and was removed by the 44th Amendment which made Cabinet advice binding without exception.

statement_analysis.statement: Since an ordinance is effectively a Cabinet decision, the Parliament can hold the Council of Ministers accountable for the ordinance through a vote of no-confidence, even before the ordinance is laid before Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliamentary accountability for executive actions — including ordinances — flows through the Cabinet's collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha under Article 75(3); Parliament can use political tools including no-confidence motions against the Cabinet for ordinance misuse at any time.

statement_analysis.statement: The Constitution explicitly provides that the President may return an ordinance proposal to the Cabinet for reconsideration, analogous to the power under Article 111 to return a Bill.
statement_analysis.reason: There is no explicit constitutional provision allowing the President to return an ordinance proposal; Article 111 applies to Bills passed by Parliament, not to Cabinet recommendations for ordinances. Any such power is at most a matter of constitutional convention, debated but not explicitly granted.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (1, 2 and 3) is a strong distractor because Statement 3 sounds authoritative — the Article 111 analogy is plausible, and students who recall that the President can return Bills may assume the same applies to ordinance proposals without checking whether there is an explicit provision.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 3: The Constitution does NOT explicitly provide for returning an ordinance proposal — Article 111 applies only to Bills passed by Parliament; Statement 3 is incorrect; eliminate all options that include Statement 3.
Evaluate Statement 1: The 44th Amendment (1978) made Cabinet advice binding — implying there was a pre-existing discretion element before 1978; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Cabinet collective responsibility under Article 75(3) means Parliament can hold Cabinet accountable through a no-confidence vote for ordinance misuse — Statement 2 is correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct; Statement 3 is incorrect — select option c (1 and 2 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a plausible-fabrication trap dressed in the language of constitutional analogy. The Article 111 power to return Bills is a well-known presidential power, and the question creates a false parallel by suggesting it explicitly extends to ordinance proposals. Students who reason by analogy rather than by constitutional text will accept Statement 3, choosing option d. The correct position is that while there is academic debate about whether such a power exists by convention, there is no explicit constitutional provision — making the statement as worded incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
The role of the Cabinet in ordinance promulgation is governed by the interaction of Articles 74 and 123.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Before the 44th Amendment, the President could send Cabinet advice back once for reconsideration — a limited discretionary element. The 44th Amendment removed this, making Cabinet advice binding in all cases, including ordinances.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Constitution's scheme of collective Cabinet responsibility (Article 75(3)) means Parliament can hold the Cabinet politically accountable for ordinances at any time — even before formal laying — through debates, questions, and ultimately a no-confidence vote.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: No explicit constitutional provision mirrors Article 111 (return of Bills) for ordinance proposals. Article 111 applies only to Bills that have passed both Houses of Parliament; it has no textual application to Cabinet recommendations for ordinances. Any Presidential hesitation on an ordinance proposal is at most a constitutional convention debated by scholars, not an express constitutional right.

Value Addition:
• Political accountability — not judicial review — is the primary real-world check on ordinance misuse.
• The Second ARC recommended mandatory certification of urgency before ordinance promulgation.
• Post-44th Amendment, even the President's request for reconsideration of Cabinet ordinance advice has no explicit constitutional basis.

solution.concept_anchor: Ordinance during Lok Sabha dissolution — laying requirement
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students who know that ordinances must be laid before Parliament assume this happens at the 'next session' of Parliament, without accounting for the fact that after dissolution, a new Lok Sabha is constituted and it is before this newly formed Lok Sabha that the ordinance must first be laid.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: 'Next session of the same Parliament' is impossible after dissolution — dissolution ends the life of the Lok Sabha; there is no 'same Parliament' to reconvene.
Eliminate option c: Laying only before the Rajya Sabha is insufficient — ordinances must be laid before both Houses; the Rajya Sabha alone cannot fulfill the mandatory laying requirement.

Eliminate option d: The ordinance does not lapse merely because Lok Sabha was dissolved — dissolution does not automatically invalidate an existing ordinance; it extends the practical life of the ordinance.
Confirm option b: After dissolution, the ordinance must be laid before the newly constituted Lok Sabha when it first meets, along with the Rajya Sabha — select option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap here exploits confusion about constitutional continuity across Lok Sabha dissolutions. Students who know that ordinances must be 'laid before Parliament when it reassembles' automatically think of the same Parliament resuming its session, not a newly constituted Lok Sabha coming into existence. The dissolution scenario is a different constitutional situation — the ordinance survives dissolution and must be placed before the new Lok Sabha at its first meeting.
solution.final_explanation:
When the President promulgates an ordinance and the Lok Sabha is dissolved before the ordinance can be laid before Parliament, a unique constitutional situation arises.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Dissolution terminates the existence of the Lok Sabha — there is no 'next session of the same Lok Sabha' to which the ordinance can be presented.
• Option (b) — Correct: The ordinance survives dissolution. When the newly constituted Lok Sabha meets for the first time after general elections, the ordinance must be laid before it (along with the Rajya Sabha). The 6-week validity period then begins from the date Parliament reassembles.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Rajya Sabha alone cannot fulfill the mandatory laying requirement. Article 123(2) requires laying before both Houses, and ordinance disapproval requires resolutions of both Houses.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: An ordinance does not lapse automatically on dissolution. Dissolution affects only the Lok Sabha's membership — not the legal validity of existing ordinances.

Value Addition:
• Dissolution vs. prorogation: prorogation ends a session; dissolution ends the entire Lok Sabha's life — a critical distinction for ordinance continuity.
• An ordinance issued just before dissolution to avoid imminent legislative rejection raises constitutional morality concerns (Krishna Kumar Singh, 2017).
• The ordinance issued during dissolution has a longer practical life — it remains valid until 6 weeks after the new Lok Sabha meets.

solution.concept_anchor: Ordinance under Article 13 — no immunity from fundamental rights review

statement_analysis.statement: A Presidential ordinance is classified as 'subordinate legislation' under Article 13 and is therefore subject to a stricter standard of judicial review than an Act of Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: An ordinance is not subordinate legislation — it has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament. Article 13 includes ordinances in the definition of 'law,' and they are subject to the same (not stricter) standard of fundamental rights review as Acts.

statement_analysis.statement: A Presidential ordinance that suspends Article 19 freedoms can remain operative during a National Emergency declared under Article 352, because the Emergency itself suspends those freedoms.
statement_analysis.reason: It is the Presidential Proclamation under Article 352 (and the consequent Article 358/359 operation) that suspends or restricts Article 19 — not the ordinance independently. An ordinance by itself cannot suspend fundamental rights; the suspension during Emergency derives from the Emergency proclamation and related constitutional provisions, not from the ordinance's own authority.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because students who know that during National Emergency, Article 19 freedoms are restricted (under Article 358) may conflate this with the ordinance being the operative instrument of suspension, rather than recognising that the Emergency proclamation itself is the source of the restriction.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Ordinances are NOT subordinate legislation — they have the same force as Acts of Parliament; the premise that they face a 'stricter standard' is false; Statement 1 is NOT correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: An ordinance cannot independently suspend Article 19 — it is the Emergency proclamation under Article 352 (operating through Articles 358/359) that restricts Article 19 during Emergency; Statement 2 is also NOT correct.
Both statements are incorrect — the question asks which are NOT correct — select option c (Both 1 and 2).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the scope-extension error of conflating 'ordinance' with 'subordinate legislation.' Students who know that rules, regulations, and notifications are subordinate legislation subject to strict review may extend this to ordinances. Statement 2 exploits the National Emergency context — students who know Article 19 is suspended during Emergency incorrectly attribute this suspension to whatever legislative instrument is active (including ordinances), rather than to the Emergency proclamation itself.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between Presidential ordinances and fundamental rights is governed by Article 13 and the general constitutional framework.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Ordinances are not subordinate legislation. Article 13(3)(a) defines 'law' to include 'any Ordinance' — placing ordinances alongside Acts in the fundamental rights review framework. They are primary legislation with the same force as an Act, not delegated/subordinate legislation. There is no stricter review standard.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: An ordinance by itself cannot suspend Article 19 freedoms. During a National Emergency declared under Article 352, it is Articles 358 and 359 — not any ordinance — that restrict or suspend Article 19 rights. A Presidential ordinance cannot independently achieve what only a constitutional proclamation can do.

Value Addition:
• Article 13(3) definition of 'law' covers: laws in force before the Constitution (clause 1), and laws made after (clause 2) — including ordinances, bylaws, orders, regulations, etc.
• An ordinance imposing reasonable restrictions under Articles 19(2)–(6) is valid; it is only an ordinance violating Part III that is void.
• Article 358 suspends Article 19 automatically during National Emergency; Article 359 allows Presidential orders to suspend the right to move courts for other fundamental rights.

solution.concept_anchor: Ordinance Raj — reform recommendations and constitutional morality

statement_analysis.statement: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission (Second ARC) recommended that the government should provide a mandatory statement of urgency explaining why an ordinance was necessary whenever it promulgates one.
statement_analysis.reason: The Second ARC recommended stricter guidelines for ordinance use, including mandatory certification of urgency, to prevent misuse and ensure transparency in executive legislation.

statement_analysis.statement: The Law Commission of India has recommended that any ordinance not converted into an Act by Parliament should automatically become permanently void with retrospective effect from the date of promulgation.
statement_analysis.reason: While the Law Commission has recommended stricter ordinance guidelines, no recommendation provides for retrospective voidance from the date of promulgation — acts done under the ordinance during its currency are generally protected; the Law Commission's recommendations do not include automatic retrospective invalidation.

statement_analysis.statement: Data from India's legislative history shows that a significant proportion of Presidential ordinances lapse without being converted into Acts of Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: Analysis of ordinance use in India consistently shows that many ordinances are not converted into Acts, either because Parliament is not in session long enough or because political will to pass legislation is absent — a key basis for the 'Ordinance Raj' critique.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court in Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) held that the President must personally certify in writing that he/she is satisfied about the urgency before promulgating an ordinance.
statement_analysis.reason: Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) addressed the bona fide nature of satisfaction and re-promulgation but did not prescribe a specific written certification requirement by the President personally — such a requirement does not exist in constitutional text or in the ruling.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Only three) is a strong distractor because statements 1, 2, and 3 together sound like a coherent set of reform measures; students who do not carefully parse the retrospective voidance element in Statement 2 or the personal certification element in Statement 4 may accept three as correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 2: 'Automatically permanently void with retrospective effect' — this is not part of any Law Commission recommendation; acts done under a lapsed ordinance remain protected; Statement 2 is incorrect.

Evaluate Statement 4: Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) examined bona fide satisfaction but did NOT prescribe a personal written certification by the President — this is a plausible-fabrication; Statement 4 is incorrect.
Confirm Statement 1: Second ARC's mandatory urgency statement recommendation is an established reform proposal — Statement 1 is correct.

Confirm Statement 3: The data point about ordinances lapsing without conversion is well-supported in legislative studies — Statement 3 is correct. Two statements are correct — select option b (Only two).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 is a plausible-fabrication — it sounds like a reasonable constitutional safeguard that a court might impose and uses the authoritative name of Krishna Kumar Singh (2017). Students who know the case addressed presidential satisfaction but do not recall its precise holdings will accept Statement 4 as part of the ruling. Statement 2's 'retrospective void from date of promulgation' sounds like a logical consequence of non-conversion but conflicts with the well-established protection for acts done under an ordinance during its currency.
solution.final_explanation:
The 'Ordinance Raj' debate encompasses both empirical patterns of executive overreach and reform recommendations.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Second ARC recommended that when promulgating an ordinance, the government should provide a mandatory statement explaining the urgency — a transparency safeguard designed to discipline ordinance use.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: No Law Commission recommendation provides for retrospective voidance from the date of promulgation for lapsed ordinances. The standard position is that acts done under an ordinance during its currency are valid even after the ordinance lapses — retrospective invalidation is not recommended.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Data on Indian legislative practice consistently shows that many ordinances are re-promulgated or simply allowed to lapse rather than being converted into Acts through proper legislative scrutiny.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) examined whether presidential satisfaction was bona fide and held re-promulgation unconstitutional, but it did not prescribe a personal written certification requirement by the President — no such procedural mandate exists.

Value Addition:
• The 'Ordinance Raj' critique gained prominence particularly during periods of coalition politics and hung Parliaments.
• Some constitutional democracies require legislative pre-approval or post-approval within shorter windows than India's 6-week standard.
• The real accountability mechanism is political — Cabinet accountability to the Lok Sabha through collective responsibility.

concepts_used: Comparative Analysis: Article 123 vs. Article 213 (Governor's Ordinance Power)

solution.concept_anchor: Governor's ordinance — Presidential instructions requirement
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Article 213(1) contains a proviso that the Governor cannot promulgate an ordinance on certain subjects (e.g., compulsory acquisition of property, matters affecting High Court jurisdiction) without first receiving instructions from the President.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The President has no analogous constraint — his ordinance power under Article 123 is not subject to any other constitutional authority's pre-approval.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The Governor requires Presidential instructions precisely because the President has final oversight over state-level executive actions that may affect central interests; this asymmetric oversight is the direct constitutional basis for A. R correctly identifies the asymmetric oversight structure that necessitates A.
Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A — select option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap operates by having students confuse which authority requires pre-approval from which other authority. Students who know that the President has oversight over Governors sometimes incorrectly generalise this to all Governor ordinances (not just specified subjects), or they may reverse the relationship and think the Governor has some oversight role over Presidential ordinances. The specific proviso under Article 213(1) — requiring Presidential instructions for specific subjects only — is the precise knowledge point.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 213(1) and its proviso create an asymmetric oversight structure between Presidential and Governor's ordinance powers.

• Assertion (A) is correct: The Governor cannot promulgate an ordinance on certain specified subjects — notably those involving compulsory acquisition of property, matters that would derogate from the powers of the High Court, or matters on which the State Legislature would require Presidential assent — without first receiving instructions from the President. This proviso is explicit in Article 213(1).
• Reason (R) is correct: The President's own ordinance power under Article 123 has no equivalent constraint — no external constitutional authority must pre-approve a Presidential ordinance. The President (acting on Cabinet advice) is the final authority for promulgating central ordinances.
• Causal link: R directly explains A. The requirement for Presidential instructions before the Governor acts on certain subjects reflects the hierarchical federal structure in which the President exercises supervisory constitutional authority over Governors. This asymmetry — Governor needing President's clearance but President needing no one's clearance — is the direct constitutional rationale for the Governor's limitation stated in A.

Value Addition:
• Governor's ordinances may also need to be reserved for Presidential consideration in some cases — analogous to Bills under Article 200.
• President can direct the Governor to withdraw a state ordinance — no reverse power exists.
• Both President and Governor ordinances share the same 6-week post-reassembly validity period.

solution.concept_anchor: Maximum operative period of a Presidential ordinance
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (8 weeks) is a strong distractor because students confuse the 6-week post-reassembly period with some composite calculation, or confuse it with other time-period provisions in the Constitution (e.g., 8-week period in other contexts).
elimination_logic: Eliminate option b (8 weeks after reassembly): The Constitution specifies 6 weeks after Parliament reassembles — not 8 weeks; this is a temporal-swap trap.
Eliminate option c (3 months from promulgation): No fixed 3-month period from promulgation exists — the period is 6 weeks after reassembly, making the total operational period variable.
Eliminate option d (12 weeks from promulgation): Not a constitutional provision — invented to exploit vague numerical memory.

Confirm option a (6 weeks after Parliament reassembles): This is the precise constitutional text of Article 123(2) — the ordinance ceases to operate 6 weeks after Parliament reassembles; select option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap substitutes 8 weeks for the correct 6 weeks, exploiting students' general awareness that the ordinance has a short post-reassembly life without precise recall of the number. Several other constitutional provisions use different week-counts, creating fertile ground for this confusion. Students who reason 'it's something like 6–8 weeks' without precision will gravitate toward option b.
solution.final_explanation:
The validity period of a Presidential ordinance after Parliament reassembles is one of the most precisely tested numerical facts in UPSC Polity.

• Option (a) — Correct: Article 123(2) provides that an ordinance ceases to operate at the expiry of 6 weeks from the reassembly of Parliament. If both Houses reassemble on different dates, the 6 weeks run from the later date.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 8 weeks is not the constitutional period — this is a numerical trap.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: There is no fixed 3-month period measured from promulgation; the period depends on when Parliament reassembles, making the total life variable.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: 12 weeks is not a constitutional provision for ordinance validity.

Value Addition:
• The practical maximum life of an ordinance is roughly 6 months (maximum inter-session period) + 6 weeks.
• Governor's ordinance under Article 213 also ceases 6 weeks after the State Legislature reassembles — the same period applies to both.
• An ordinance can cease before 6 weeks if Parliament passes a disapproval resolution or the President withdraws it.

solution.concept_anchor: AK Roy 1982 — judicial review of presidential satisfaction

statement_analysis.statement: In AK Roy v. Union of India (1982), the Supreme Court held that presidential satisfaction under Article 123 is completely beyond the scope of judicial review under any circumstances.
statement_analysis.reason: AK Roy (1982) held precisely the opposite — presidential satisfaction is NOT immune from judicial review; the Court held it was reviewable for bona fides, though courts are reluctant to interfere in genuine urgency cases.

statement_analysis.statement: An ordinance can be challenged in court on the ground that the President lacked legislative competence to issue it on a particular subject.
statement_analysis.reason: Lack of legislative competence (e.g., issuing an ordinance on a State List subject) is a valid ground of judicial challenge — the Court can examine whether the subject-matter of the ordinance falls within Parliament's (and therefore the President's) ordinance jurisdiction.

statement_analysis.statement: An ordinance that violates a fundamental right under Part III can be struck down by a court even during the ordinance's currency.
statement_analysis.reason: Ordinances are included in Article 13's definition of 'law' — a court can strike down an ordinance that violates fundamental rights at any time during its operation, without waiting for the ordinance to lapse.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (2 and 3 only) is effectively the correct answer — but option d in a 4-statement set would normally be 1, 2 and 3. Here with 3 statements, the correct answer is option d (2 and 3 only) with the option pattern adjusted. Wait — format requires 3-statement multi-correct options: (a) 1 and 2 only, (b) 2 and 3 only, (c) 1 and 3 only, (d) 1, 2 and 3. Correct answer is b (2 and 3 only). Correction: correct_option should be b.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: AK Roy (1982) held presidential satisfaction IS reviewable — the statement claims it is completely beyond review, which is directly contrary to the ruling; Statement 1 is incorrect; eliminate all options including Statement 1.
Evaluate Statement 2: Lack of legislative competence is a recognised ground of challenge for ordinances — courts can examine subject-matter jurisdiction; Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 13 includes ordinances in 'law' — fundamental rights challenges against ordinances are maintainable during the ordinance's currency; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct; Statement 1 is incorrect — select option b (2 and 3 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits a partial-truth about presidential satisfaction. Students who know that 'presidential satisfaction is subjective' and that 'courts are reluctant to interfere with executive urgency judgments' may incorrectly generalise this into 'completely beyond judicial review.' The actual holding in AK Roy (1982) is the opposite — the Court asserted the power of review but exercised restraint in the specific case. The distinction between 'reviewable but restrained' and 'immune from review' is the precise knowledge point that separates well-prepared candidates.
solution.final_explanation:
Judicial review of Presidential ordinances operates across multiple grounds, and the scope of this review was crystallised by AK Roy (1982) and Krishna Kumar Singh (2017).

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: AK Roy v. Union of India (1982) explicitly held that presidential satisfaction is NOT immune from judicial review. The Court can examine whether the satisfaction was bona fide. The Court's reluctance to interfere does not translate into a legal bar on review — the power of review exists but is exercised with restraint.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Legislative competence is always a justiciable question. If the President issues an ordinance on a State List subject (outside Parliament's competence), a court can strike it down on competence grounds — the same jurisdictional analysis that applies to Acts.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Since Article 13(3)(a) expressly includes 'Ordinance' in its definition of 'law,' a court can declare an ordinance void if it violates fundamental rights — and can do so while the ordinance is still in force.

Value Addition:
• Grounds of challenge: malafide exercise, lack of competence, violation of Part III, and (post-Krishna Kumar Singh) lack of genuine urgency.
• Courts distinguish between 'propriety' (not reviewable) and 'constitutionality' (fully reviewable) of ordinances.
• An unconstitutional ordinance is void ab initio — acts done under it may also be challenged.

solution.concept_anchor: Ordinance cannot amend Constitution — absolute bar vs. ordinary Acts

statement_analysis.statement: A Presidential ordinance can amend or repeal any existing ordinary Act of Parliament on a subject within Parliament's legislative competence, and such amendment has the same legal effect as an amendment made by Parliament itself.
statement_analysis.reason: An ordinance having 'the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament' necessarily means it can amend or repeal existing Acts on competent subjects during its currency — this is the direct consequence of equal legal standing.

statement_analysis.statement: A Presidential ordinance can amend the Constitution if the proposed amendment does not require a Special Majority, since ordinary legislative majority is sufficient for non-special-majority amendments.
statement_analysis.reason: No constitutional amendment — whether or not it requires a Special Majority — can be achieved through an ordinance. Article 368 prescribes a specific legislative process (bicameral passage, special majority, and sometimes state ratification) for all constitutional amendments. Ordinance power is legislative substitute power, not constituent power, and this bar is absolute regardless of the type of majority involved.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is clearly correct, and students who partially know that 'some constitutional amendments require only simple majority' (e.g., Article 368's reference to ordinary provisions) may incorrectly reason that an ordinance substituting for a simple majority law could also achieve a simple-majority constitutional amendment.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Equal legal force means an ordinance can amend existing Acts — this is a well-established consequence of Article 123; Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The claim that ordinances can achieve non-Special-Majority constitutional amendments is the scope-extension error — the bar on ordinances amending the Constitution is absolute, applying to all categories of amendments regardless of majority type; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option c (Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 exploits knowledge of constitutional amendment categories. Students who know that some constitutional provisions can be amended by ordinary majority (Parliament alone, no special majority needed) extend this logic to conclude that if the ordinary legislative process can achieve it, an ordinance — which substitutes for ordinary legislation — can also achieve it. The fatal flaw in this reasoning is that constitutional amendment power (Article 368) and ordinary legislative power (Article 107 and its ordinance substitute, Article 123) are separate constitutional powers with separate procedures. Even 'simple majority' amendments go through the Article 368 process — they are not ordinary legislation.
solution.final_explanation:
This question probes the boundary between what an ordinance can do (substitute for ordinary legislation) and what it cannot do (exercise constituent power).

• Statement 1 — Correct: An ordinance's equal legal force with an Act of Parliament means it can amend, modify, or repeal existing parliamentary Acts on competent subjects during its operation. This is not a theoretical possibility but a direct textual consequence of Article 123's 'same force and effect' language.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The distinction between 'ordinary majority amendments' and 'special majority amendments' is irrelevant to the ordinance bar. ALL constitutional amendments — whether they require a simple majority, a special majority, or state ratification — must go through the Article 368 procedure. This is because constitutional amendment is an exercise of constituent power, not legislative power. An ordinance can only substitute for legislative power — it has no access to constituent power under any circumstances.

Value Addition:
• Examples of constitutional provisions amendable by simple majority: changing state boundaries (Article 4), abolishing or creating Legislative Councils (Article 169) — even these cannot be done by ordinance.
• The distinction: 'legislative substitute power' (Article 123) vs. 'constituent power' (Article 368) is the foundational conceptual divide.
• This limitation makes ordinance power a 'temporary legislative bridge,' not a constitutional rewriting tool.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 356 — President legislates for State via ordinance
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because students who know Article 352 expands Parliament's power to the State List may confuse Article 356 (President's Rule, which allows Presidential ordinances for a State) with Article 352 (National Emergency, which expands Parliament's legislative power but does not by itself make Presidential ordinances applicable to State matters without Parliament's session condition being met).
elimination_logic: Eliminate option b: Article 352 National Emergency expands Parliament's legislative power to the State List — but the President exercises State Legislature functions through Article 356 (President's Rule), not Article 352; this is the conflation the question targets.

Eliminate option c: An ordinance cannot be issued on State List subjects merely because the Rajya Sabha is in session — the Rajya Sabha being in session is irrelevant to the ordinance power expanding to State subjects; subject-matter jurisdiction is the controlling question.

Eliminate option d: The Governor, not having resigned, is still in place — but under Article 356, State Legislature functions are assumed by Parliament/President, allowing Presidential ordinance for the State even with a Governor in post.

Confirm option a: Under Article 356 (President's Rule in Rajasthan), the President can exercise the State Legislature's functions — this includes issuing ordinances on subjects within the State Legislature's competence; select option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges Article 352 (National Emergency) with Article 356 (President's Rule) as mechanisms through which the President can legislate on State matters by ordinance. Article 356, not Article 352, is what enables the President to assume the State Legislature's functions and issue ordinances for a State. Students who know 'National Emergency = expanded legislative power to Centre' incorrectly apply this to explain Presidential state-level ordinances, when the correct constitutional route is Article 356.
solution.final_explanation:
Under President's Rule (Article 356) in Rajasthan, Parliament assumes the State Legislature's functions. The applicable constitutional principle is Article 357, which provides that Parliament or the President (acting on Parliament's behalf) can exercise the State Legislature's powers during President's Rule.

The scenario asks which provision authorises the President to issue an ordinance on a State subject while Rajasthan is under President's Rule and Parliament is in recess.

• Option (a) — Correct: Under Article 356, the President assumes the State Legislature's functions. This means the President can issue ordinances on subjects within Rajasthan's State List — an exception to the normal rule that Presidential ordinances cover only Union and Concurrent List subjects. The route is Article 356 read with Article 357, not any emergency expansion.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Article 352 National Emergency expands Parliament's legislative power to the State List — but this is a different mechanism and does not by itself create Presidential ordinance power over a specific State's subjects during that State's President's Rule.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Rajya Sabha being in session is a condition for Parliamentary recess analysis — it does not independently authorise the President to issue ordinances on State subjects.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Governor's continued presence does not preclude Presidential ordinance power under Article 356 — the two are not mutually exclusive.

Value Addition:
• Parliament can also pass laws directly for a State under President's Rule — both routes (Presidential ordinance and Parliamentary legislation) exist under Article 357.
• Such laws made during President's Rule continue in force after the President's Rule ends, until the State Legislature amends or repeals them.
• Article 358/359 (Emergency fundamental rights provisions) are distinct from Article 356's legislative power assumption.
